description: We are doing kerbal space program's launch gap planning and orbit setting stage, please join us if you want to!
summary:
We made a game where you get to be the mission planner. You start small, by getting a satellite into orbit around Earth, then work your way up to landing on the Moon, building a base on Mars and eventually terraforming it.
Everything runs on publicly available NASA data. The planets, Pluto and the Moon are exactly where NASA JPL's DE440 data says they are on any date, so when you plan a trip to Mars, you're working with the real Mars. Out of the six stages of mission planning, we focused on two: picking the launch window and trajectory, and the logistics of keeping a mission alive (fuel, food, water, power, crew and money).
When you're new, a pop-up guide walks you through your first mission step by step. After every mission you get a report and a score that tells you what went well and what to fix. We wanted people to understand why real missions are planned the way they are, by trying it themselves.
details:
How it works: you see the solar system live in 3D, with every planet placed using NASA JPL's DE440 data. You open the mission planner, pick a rocket, an engine, fuel, crew and things to carry (habitats, supplies, solar panels, satellites), and then find a launch window. The game shows you a "porkchop" chart of every departure date and flight time, so you can pick the cheapest or the fastest trip. Your craft then flies using real orbital physics, including gravity assists off other planets.

We simulate 2 of the 6 stages of mission planning: launch window and trajectory design, and mission logistics. Crews eat and drink every day, bases need power, and every launch costs money, so a plan that looks fine on paper can still fail if you run out of water on the way.

Levels go from Tutorial (put a satellite in orbit) to Easy (land on the Moon and come home), Medium (keep four people alive on Mars for a year) and Hard (terraform Mars in three stages). Exploring somewhere for the first time earns science points, which unlock better engines and modules. Every finished mission, whether it worked or not, gets a report that explains what happened and how to do better.

Why we think it matters: most people never see how much planning goes into a real mission. Here you learn it by trying, failing and trying again, using the same kind of data NASA's planners use.

What we used: Python, Ursina and Panda3D for the 3D view, Tkinter for the windows, NumPy, and SpiceyPy to read NASA's SPICE data files. uv makes it a one-command install.

What we thought about: keeping the physics accurate while still making it fun, making it friendly for complete beginners, and making sure it runs smoothly on normal laptops.
projectRefs: Kerbal Space Program (inspiration for spacecraft navigation and mission planning)
Solar Expanse (inspiration for logistics and base management)
